column2: And to the Aeolian island we came; and there dwelt
Aeolus son of Hippotas, dear to the immortal gods,
on a floating island; and all around it a wall
of bronze, unbreakable, and a smooth rock runs up.
His twelve children too were born in the halls,
six daughters, and six sons in their prime;
there he gave his daughters to his sons to be wives.
And they always beside their dear father and careful mother
feast, and beside them lie countless good things,
and the savoury house resounds all around in the courtyard
by day; and by night again beside their respected wives
they sleep, on rugs and on bedsteads with holes bored for cords.
And indeed to their city we came and their fair house.
A whole month he entertained me and asked about each thing,
Ilios and the ships of the Argives and the return of the Achaeans;
and I too told him everything in due order.
But when I too asked for the road and urged him
to send me on, he refused nothing, but prepared the sending.
And he gave me a bag, having flayed an ox of nine years,
and in it he bound the paths of the blustering winds;
for the son of Kronos had made him steward of the winds,
both to still them and to rouse them, whichever he wishes.
And in the hollow ship he bound it with a shining cord
of silver, so that not even a little might blow out;
but for me he sent forth the breath of Zephyrus to blow,
that it might carry both ships and men themselves; yet it was not to
be accomplished; for we perished through our own folly.
For nine days we sailed alike by night and day,
and on the tenth the fatherland's fields already appeared,
and we saw, being near, men tending fires.
Then sweet sleep came upon me, exhausted,
for I was always handling the ship's sheet, and to no other
of my comrades gave it, so that we might reach our fatherland sooner.
But my comrades spoke to one another with words,
and said that I was taking home gold and silver
as gifts from great-hearted Aeolus son of Hippotas.
And so one would say, looking at his neighbour:

Alas, how dear and honoured this man is
39	to all men, to whatever city and land he comes.
40	Many fair treasures he takes from Troy
41	from the spoil, while we, having completed the same journey,
42	go home with empty hands;
43	and now Aeolus has given him these things, favouring him out of friendship.
44	But come, let us quickly see what these are,
45	how much gold and silver there is in the bag.
So they said, and the evil counsel of the comrades prevailed;
they untied the bag, and all the winds rushed out.
And at once a gale seized them and bore them to the sea
weeping, away from their fatherland. But I,
waking, pondered in my blameless heart
whether I should fall from the ship and perish in the sea,
or endure in silence and still be among the living.
But I endured and stayed, and covering myself I lay
in the ship. And the ships were carried by the evil blast of wind
back again to the Aeolian island, and my comrades groaned.
There we went onto the mainland and drew water,
and at once my comrades took a meal beside the swift ships.
But when we had had our fill of food and drink,
then I, taking with me a herald and one comrade,
went to the famous house of Aeolus; and I found him
feasting beside his wife and his children.
And coming to the house, by the doorposts on the threshold
we sat; and they were amazed in their hearts and questioned:

How have you come, Odysseus? What evil spirit assailed you?
65	Surely we sent you off with care, so that you might reach
66	your fatherland and house and wherever is dear to you.
So they said, and I spoke among them, grieved at heart:

My wretched comrades ruined me, and besides them cruel
69	sleep. But heal it, friends; for the power is in you.
So I spoke, addressing them with soft words,
but they became silent; and the father answered with a word:

Get out of the island quickly, most disgraceful of the living;
73	for it is not right for me to entertain or to send off
74	the man who is hated by the blessed gods.
75	Get out, since you come here hated by the gods.
So saying he sent me from the house, groaning heavily.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart.
And the men's spirit was worn by the grievous rowing
through our own folly, since no escort appeared any more.
For six days we sailed alike by night and day,
and on the seventh we came to the steep citadel of Lamos,
Telepylos of the Laestrygonians, where shepherd calls to shepherd
as he drives in, and the one driving out answers.
There a sleepless man could have earned double wages,
one tending cattle, the other pasturing white sheep;
for the paths of night and day are close.
There when we came to the famous harbour, around which a rock
sheer runs unbroken on both sides,
and projecting headlands facing one another
stand out at the mouth, and the entrance is narrow,
there they all brought their curved ships inside.
And these were tied inside the hollow harbour
close together; for no wave ever rose in it,
neither big nor small, but a white calm was all around.
But I alone held my black ship outside,
there at the very edge, having tied the cables to the rock;
and I stood, going up onto a rugged lookout.
There no works of oxen or of men appeared,
but we see only smoke leaping up from the earth.
Then I sent comrades ahead to go and find out
who the men were who ate bread upon the earth,
choosing two men, and adding a herald as the third.
And they went ashore along a smooth road, on which wagons
brought timber down to the city from the high mountains,
and they met a girl before the city drawing water,
the daughter of the mighty Laestrygonian Antiphates.
She had come down to the fair-flowing spring
Artakia; for from there they carried water to the city.
And they stood by her and spoke to her and asked
who was king of these people and over whom he ruled;
and she at once pointed out her father's high-roofed house.
And when they entered the famous house, they found the woman,
as big as a mountain peak, and they loathed her.
And she at once called from the assembly famous Antiphates,
her husband, who devised for them grievous destruction.
At once he seized one of the comrades and prepared a meal;
and the other two, darting off in flight, reached the ships.
But he raised a shout through the city; and hearing it
the mighty Laestrygonians came crowding, one from here, one from there,
countless, not like men but like Giants.
They from the rocks with stones that a man could lift
pelted; and at once an evil din arose along the ships
of men being destroyed and ships at once being shattered;
and like fishes spearing them they carried off a joyless feast.
While they were destroying these inside the deep harbour,
meanwhile I, drawing my sharp sword from beside my thigh,
with it cut the cables of the dark-prowed ship.
And at once urging my comrades I ordered them
to fall to the oars, so that we might escape from evil;
and they all tossed up the brine, fearing destruction.
And gladly out to sea, away from the overhanging rocks,
my ship fled; but the others perished all together there.
From there we sailed on further, grieved at heart,
glad to have escaped death, though we had lost dear comrades.
And to the Aeaean island we came; and there dwelt
Circe of the fair tresses, a dread goddess with human speech,
own sister of baleful-minded Aietes;
both were born of Helios who gives light to mortals
and of their mother Perse, whom Okeanos begot as a child.
There we put in with the ship in silence on the shore
to a harbour good for ships, and some god was leading.
There then, going ashore, for two days and two nights
we lay together, eating our hearts with weariness and pains.
But when fair-tressed Dawn brought the third day to its end,
then I, taking my spear and sharp sword,
quickly went up from the ship to a lookout,
in case I might see works of mortals and hear a voice.
And I stood, going up onto a rugged lookout,
and smoke appeared to me from the broad-pathed earth,
in the halls of Circe, through thick bushes and forest.
Then I pondered in my mind and in my heart
whether to go and inquire, since I had seen the blazing smoke.
And as I thought, this seemed to me the better course,
first to go to the swift ship and the sea-shore,
give my comrades a meal and send them to inquire.
But when, going, I was already near the curved ship,
then some god pitied me, being alone,
who sent me a great high-antlered stag onto the very road.
It was coming down to the river from its woodland pasture
to drink; for the force of the sun held it.
And as it came out I struck it in the middle of the back
by the spine; and the bronze spear passed straight through,
and it fell in the dust bellowing, and its life flew away.
Then I, stepping on it, drew the bronze spear
from the wound; that I laid down there on the ground
and left; but I pulled up twigs and willow shoots,
and, as much as a fathom, a well-twisted rope
I plaited at both ends and bound the feet of the dreadful monster,
and went, carrying it over my neck, to the black ship
leaning on my spear, since it was not at all possible
to carry it on my shoulder with the other hand; for it was a very great beast.
I threw it down before the ship, and roused my comrades
with honeyed words, standing by each man:

Friends, we shall not yet go down, grieved though we are,
175	into the house of Hades, before the day of fate comes;
176	but come, while there is food and drink in the swift ship,
177	let us think of eating, and not be worn out with hunger.
So I spoke, and they quickly obeyed my words,
and uncovering themselves beside the shore of the barren sea
they gazed at the stag; for it was a very great beast.
But when they had delighted their eyes with the sight,
washing their hands they prepared a splendid feast.
So then for the whole day until the sun went down
we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and darkness came on,
then we lay down to sleep on the breaking edge of the sea.
And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
then I, calling an assembly, spoke among them all:

Hear my words, comrades, though you suffer evils;
190	friends, for we do not know where is the gloom nor where the dawn,
191	nor where the sun that gives light to mortals goes under the earth,
192	nor where it rises; but let us consider quickly
193	whether there will yet be any plan. I do not think there is.
194	For I saw, going up to a rugged lookout,
195	an island, which the boundless sea wreathes all around;
196	and it itself lies low; and in the middle a smoke
197	I saw with my eyes through thick bushes and forest.
So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken
as they remembered the deeds of Laestrygonian Antiphates
and of the Cyclops' violence, the great-hearted man-eater.
They wept shrilly, shedding warm tears;
but no profit came to them from lamenting.
But I counted all my well-greaved comrades
in two groups, and gave a leader to each of the two;
of one I was leader, and of the other godlike Eurylochus.
And we quickly shook lots in a bronze-covered helmet;
and out leapt the lot of great-hearted Eurylochus.
He went, and with him two and twenty comrades
weeping; and they left us behind lamenting.
And they found in the glens Circe's house, built
of polished stones, in a place with a wide view;
and around it were mountain wolves and lions,
whom she herself had bewitched, since she had given them evil drugs.
And these did not rush upon the men, but
rose up fawning with their long tails.
As when dogs fawn around their master coming from a feast,
for he always brings morsels to soothe their hearts,
so around them wolves with strong claws and lions
fawned; and they were afraid, when they saw the dreadful monsters.
And they stood in the forecourt of the fair-tressed goddess,
and within they heard Circe singing with a beautiful voice,
going to and fro at a great immortal web, such as the works of goddesses are,
fine and graceful and splendid.
And among them Polites, leader of men, began to speak,
who was dearest of my comrades and most trusty to me:

Friends, for inside someone going to and fro at a great web
227	sings beautifully, and the whole floor echoes around,
228	either a goddess or a woman; but let us call out quickly.
So he spoke, and they called out, shouting.
And she at once came out and opened the shining doors
and invited them; and all together they followed in their ignorance;
but Eurylochus stayed behind, suspecting a trick.
And leading them in she seated them on couches and chairs,
and for them cheese and barley meal and yellow honey
with Pramnian wine she mixed; and she mixed into the food
baneful drugs, so that they might utterly forget their fatherland.
But when she had given it and they had drunk it down, at once then
striking them with a wand she shut them in the pigsties.
And they had the heads of swine, and the voice and bristles
and the form, but their mind was steadfast, as before.
So they were shut in weeping, and Circe threw before them
acorn and mast and the fruit of the cornel
to eat, such as swine that lie on the ground always eat.
And Eurylochus came at once to the swift black ship
to tell the news of his comrades and their bitter fate.
Nor could he utter a single word, though he longed to,
struck at heart with great grief; and his eyes
were filled with tears, and his spirit foresaw lamentation.
But when we all in amazement questioned him,
then he told of the destruction of the other comrades:

We went, as you ordered, through the bushes, glorious Odysseus;
252	we found in the glens a fair house built
253	of polished stones, in a place with a wide view.
254	There someone going to and fro at a great web sang clearly,
255	either a goddess or a woman; and they called out, shouting.
256	And she at once came out and opened the shining doors
257	and invited them; and all together they followed in their ignorance;
258	but I stayed behind, suspecting a trick.
259	And they all together vanished, and none of them
260	appeared; and I watched for a long time, sitting.
So he spoke, but I slung around my shoulders my silver-studded sword,
great, of bronze, and the bow beside it;
and I bade him lead me back by the same road.
But he, grasping my knees with both hands, begged,
and lamenting spoke to me winged words:

Do not take me there against my will, Zeus-nurtured, but leave me here.
267	For I know that you will neither come back yourself nor bring any other
268	of your comrades. But with these here let us quickly
269	flee; for still we might escape the evil day.
So he spoke, and I answered him and said:
So saying I went up away from the ship and the sea.
But when, going through the sacred glens, I was about
to reach the great house of Circe of many drugs,
there Hermes of the golden wand met me
as I was going to the house, like a young man,
with the first down on his lip, whose youth is most graceful;
and he clasped my hand, and spoke a word and addressed me:

Where now again, unhappy man, are you going over the hills alone,
282	ignorant of the place? And these comrades of yours in Circe's house
283	are penned like swine, having thick lairs.
284	Do you come here to free them? I say you will not
285	return yourself, but will stay there, where the others are.
286	But come, I shall release you from the evils and save you.
287	Here, take this good drug and go to the house of Circe,
288	which will keep the evil day from your head.
289	And I shall tell you all the baleful devices of Circe.
290	She will make you a potion, and cast drugs into the food.
291	But even so she will not be able to bewitch you; for the good drug
292	which I shall give you will not allow it; and I shall tell you each thing.
293	Whenever Circe strikes you with her long wand,
294	then you, drawing your sharp sword from beside your thigh,
295	rush at Circe, as if eager to kill her.
296	And she, fearing, will bid you lie with her;
297	then do not any longer refuse the goddess's bed,
298	so that she may free your comrades and take care of you yourself;
299	but bid her swear a great oath by the blessed ones,
300	that she will not plan some other evil harm against you,
301	lest, when you are stripped, she make you cowardly and unmanned.
So having spoken, the Argeiphontes gave me the drug,
pulling it from the earth, and showed me its nature.
At the root it was black, and the flower was like milk;
moly the gods call it; and it is hard to dig up
for mortal men, but the gods can do all things.
Then Hermes went away to high Olympus
across the wooded island, and I to the house of Circe
went, and my heart surged much as I went.
And I stood at the doors of the fair-tressed goddess;
standing there I shouted, and the goddess heard my voice.
And she at once came out and opened the shining doors
and invited me; and I followed, grieved at heart.
Leading me in she seated me on a silver-studded chair,
fair, richly wrought; and a footstool was beneath my feet;
and she made me a potion in a golden cup, that I might drink,
and put the drug in, devising evil in her heart.
But when she had given it and I drank it down, and it did not bewitch me,
striking me with her wand she spoke a word and addressed me:
Go now to the sty, lie down with your other comrades.
So she spoke, but I, drawing my sharp sword from beside my thigh,
rushed at Circe, as if eager to kill her.
And she with a great cry ran under and grasped my knees,
and lamenting spoke to me winged words:

Who are you among men, and from where? Where is your city and parents?
326	Wonder holds me that you were not bewitched, having drunk these drugs;
327	for no other man has ever endured these drugs,
328	who has drunk, and the barrier of his teeth has first passed.
329	But in your breast there is a mind that cannot be charmed.
330	Surely you are Odysseus of many turns, of whom the gold-wand
331	Argeiphontes always told me that he would come,
332	returning from Troy with his swift black ship.
333	But come now, put your sword in its sheath, and let us then
334	go up onto our bed, so that, mingling
335	in bed and love, we may trust each other.
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:

O Circe, how do you bid me be gentle to you,
338	you who turned my comrades into swine in your halls,
339	and keeping me here, with treacherous thoughts you bid me
340	go into the chamber and mount your bed,
341	so that, when I am stripped, you may make me cowardly and unmanned.
342	And I would not be willing to mount your bed,
343	unless you, goddess, would dare to swear a great oath
344	that you will not plan some other evil harm against me.
So I spoke, and she at once swore, as I bade.
But when she had sworn and completed the oath,
then I mounted the very beautiful bed of Circe.
Meanwhile the handmaids were busy in the halls,
four, who are her servants about the house;
they are born of springs and groves
and of the sacred rivers that flow out to the sea.
Of these one threw fair coverlets over the chairs,
purple on top, and spread linen beneath;
and another drew up silver tables
before the chairs, and set golden baskets on them;
and the third mixed honey-sweet wine in a bowl,
sweet, in a silver one, and distributed golden cups;
and the fourth carried water and kindled a fire
great under a big tripod; and the water grew warm.
But when the water boiled in the gleaming bronze,
she set me in a bath and washed me from the great tripod,
mixing it pleasantly, over my head and shoulders,
until she took from my limbs the spirit-wasting weariness.
But when she had washed me and anointed me richly with oil,
and cast around me a fair cloak and a tunic,
leading me in she seated me on a silver-studded chair,
fair, richly wrought, and a footstool was beneath my feet;
and a handmaid poured water for the hands from a jug, bringing it
in a fair golden one, over a silver basin,
to wash; and she drew up a polished table beside.
And the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by,
adding many dishes, giving freely of what was there.
She bade me eat; but it did not please my heart,
but I sat with my mind elsewhere, and my heart foreboded evils.
And when Circe saw me sitting, and not putting my hands
to the food, and holding strong grief,
standing near she spoke to me winged words:

Why, Odysseus, do you sit thus like one who is speechless,
379	eating your heart, and touch neither food nor drink?
380	Surely you suspect some other trick; but you need not
381	fear; for already I have sworn you a strong oath.
So she spoke, and I answered her and said:

O Circe, what man who was righteous
384	would dare to partake of food and drink
385	before he had freed his comrades and seen them with his eyes?
386	But if you bid me in good will to drink and eat,
387	free them, that I may see my trusty comrades with my eyes.
So I spoke, and Circe went out through the hall
holding her wand in her hand, and opened the doors of the sty,
and drove out creatures like fatted swine of nine years.
They then stood facing her, and she, going through them,
anointed each with another drug.
And from their limbs the bristles fell off, which before the baneful
drug had grown, which lady Circe had given them;
and they became men again, younger than before,
and much fairer and taller to look at.
And they knew me, and each clung to my hands.
And upon all came a longing sobbing, and the house around
resounded terribly; and the goddess herself pitied them.
And standing near me she spoke, bright among goddesses:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
402	go now to the swift ship and the sea-shore.
403	First of all, drag the ship up onto the land,
404	and stow the goods in caves, and all the gear;
405	and come back yourself and bring your trusty comrades.
So she spoke, and my proud heart obeyed;
and I went to the swift ship and the sea-shore.
Then I found by the swift ship my trusty comrades
piteously lamenting, shedding warm tears.
As when country calves around the cows of the herd,
coming to the yard, when they have fed their fill on pasture,
all together frisk to meet them; and no longer do the pens
hold them, but lowing continually they run about
their mothers; so they, when they saw me with their eyes,
poured around me in tears; and it seemed to their hearts
that it was as if they had reached their fatherland and the city itself
of rugged Ithaca, where they were reared and born.
And lamenting they spoke to me winged words:
So they said, and I spoke to them with soft words:

First of all let us drag the ship up onto the land,
424	and stow the goods in caves, and all the gear;
425	and you yourselves, rouse yourselves all to follow with me,
426	so that you may see your comrades in the sacred house of Circe
427	drinking and eating; for they have plenty.
So I spoke, and they quickly obeyed my words.
But Eurylochus alone tried to hold back all my comrades;
and he spoke to them winged words:

Ah, wretches, where are we going? Why do you long for these evils,
432	to go down to the hall of Circe, who will make us all
433	either swine or wolves or lions,
434	to guard her great house even under compulsion,
435	as the Cyclops did, when into his yard came
436	our comrades, and the bold Odysseus went with them;
437	for through this man's recklessness they too perished.
So he spoke, but I pondered in my mind
whether to draw my long-edged sword from beside my stout thigh
and with it strike off his head and bring it to the ground,
though he was a kinsman, and very near; but my comrades
restrained me with honeyed words, one from here, one from there:
So saying they went up away from the ship and the sea.
Nor was Eurylochus left behind by the hollow ship,
but followed; for he feared my terrible rebuke.
Meanwhile Circe in the house had bathed the other comrades
with care and anointed them richly with oil,
and cast around them woollen cloaks and tunics;
and we found them all feasting well in the halls.
And when they saw one another and looked face to face,
they wept, lamenting, and the house groaned around.
And standing near me she spoke, bright among goddesses:

No longer now stir up warm lamentation; I know myself
458	both what pains you suffered on the fishy sea,
459	and what hostile men did you harm upon the land.
460	But come, eat food and drink wine,
461	until you take heart again in your breasts,
462	such as when you first left your fatherland
463	of rugged Ithaca. But now you are dried up and spiritless,
464	always remembering the hard wandering, and never to you
465	is there joy in your heart, since you have suffered very much.
So she spoke, and our proud heart obeyed.
There then for all the days, to the full circle of a year,
we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
but when a year was complete, and the seasons turned
as the months waned, and the long days were fulfilled,
then my trusty comrades called me out and said:

Strange man, now at last remember your fatherland,
473	if it is fated for you to be saved and to reach
474	your high-roofed house and your fatherland.
So they said, and my proud heart obeyed.
So then for the whole day until the sun went down
we sat feasting on endless meat and sweet wine;
and when the sun went down and darkness came on,
they lay down to sleep through the shadowy halls.
But I, mounting the very beautiful bed of Circe,
besought her by her knees, and the goddess heard my voice;
and I spoke to her winged words:

O Circe, fulfil for me the promise which you promised,
484	to send me home; for my spirit is already eager,
485	and that of the other comrades, who wear away my dear heart
486	lamenting around me, whenever you are away.
So I spoke, and she at once answered, bright among goddesses:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
489	no longer now stay in my house against your will.
490	But first you must complete another journey and come
491	to the house of Hades and dread Persephone,
492	to consult the spirit of Theban Teiresias,
493	the blind seer, whose wits are steadfast;
494	to him, even dead, Persephone gave mind,
495	to him alone to have sense, while the others flit as shadows.
So she spoke, but my dear heart was broken;
and I wept, sitting on the bed, nor did my heart
wish any longer to live and see the light of the sun.
But when I had had my fill of weeping and rolling about,
then I answered her and said:

O Circe, who will guide this journey?
502	To Hades no one has ever yet come in a black ship.
So I spoke, and she at once answered, bright among goddesses:

Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus of many devices,
505	let no longing for a guide trouble you beside the ship,
506	but, setting up the mast and spreading the white sails,
507	sit; and the breath of Boreas will carry her for you.
508	But when in your ship you have crossed through Okeanos,
509	where is a level shore and the groves of Persephone,
510	tall poplars and willows that shed their fruit,
511	beach your ship there on deep-eddying Okeanos,
512	and go yourself to the dank house of Hades.
513	There into Acheron flow Pyriphlegethon
514	and Cocytus, which is a branch of the water of Styx,
515	and a rock, and the meeting of two roaring rivers.
516	There then, hero, drawing near, as I bid you,
517	dig a pit, a cubit's length each way,
518	and around it pour a libation to all the dead,
519	first with honeyed milk, then with sweet wine,
520	a third time with water; and sprinkle on it white barley.
521	And entreat much the strengthless heads of the dead,
522	promising, when you come to Ithaca, to sacrifice a barren cow, the best,
523	in your halls, and to fill the pyre with good things,
524	and to Teiresias apart to sacrifice a ram,
525	all black, which stands out among your flocks.
526	But when you have prayed with vows to the famous tribes of the dead,
527	then sacrifice a ram and a black ewe,
528	turning them towards Erebos, and yourself turn away,
529	making for the streams of the river; and there many
530	spirits of the dead who have died will come.
531	Then urge your comrades and exhort them
532	to flay the sheep which lie slain by the pitiless bronze,
533	and burn them, and pray to the gods,
534	to mighty Hades and dread Persephone;
535	and yourself, drawing your sharp sword from beside your thigh,
536	sit, and do not let the strengthless heads of the dead
537	come nearer the blood, before you have asked Teiresias.
538	Then at once the seer will come, leader of the people,
539	who will tell you the way and the measures of the journey
540	and the return, how you will go over the fishy sea.
So she spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
And she clothed me about in a cloak and a tunic as garments;
and the nymph herself put on a great silver-white robe,
fine and graceful, and around her waist threw
a fair golden belt, and on her head set a veil.
But I, going through the house, urged on my comrades
with honeyed words, standing by each man:

No longer now sleep and slumber in sweet sleep,
549	but let us go; for lady Circe has told me.
So I spoke, and their proud heart obeyed.
Yet not even from there did I lead my comrades unharmed.
There was one Elpenor, the youngest, not very
valiant in war nor sound in his wits;
who, apart from his comrades, in the sacred house of Circe,
longing for the cool, had lain down, heavy with wine.
And hearing the din and tramp of his comrades moving,
he suddenly leapt up, and forgot in his mind
to go back down by the long ladder,
but fell straight off the roof; and his neck
was broken from the vertebrae, and his spirit went down to Hades.
And to them as they went I spoke a word:

You think, no doubt, that you are going home
563	to your dear fatherland; but Circe has marked out another road for us,
564	to the house of Hades and dread Persephone,
565	to consult the spirit of Theban Teiresias.
So I spoke, and their dear hearts were broken,
and sitting down there they wailed and tore their hair;
but no profit came to them from lamenting.
But when to the swift ship and the sea-shore
we went, grieving, shedding warm tears,
meanwhile Circe, having gone, had tied beside the black ship
a ram and a black ewe,
easily passing by; for who could see a god who does not wish it
with his eyes, going here or there?
